No, it may be a valid extreme heat day.
It should be capped at 40C.
It can be ignored in analysis.

questions.explanation: A high temperature may be a valid extreme or a sensor error, so it needs verification rather than automatic treatment.

questions.topic: Why distance-based methods need a common scale
questions.stem: In an unscaled two-feature dataset, nearest neighbours are determined by one feature only. Why?

options.text: The other feature is constant.
That feature is more predictive by design.
That feature's scale dwarfs the other, dominating distance.
Distance methods always use one feature.

questions.explanation: The feature with the larger scale dominates Euclidean distance, making the other irrelevant. Scaling restores balance.

questions.topic: Why gradient methods need a common scale
questions.stem: Which problem is most directly caused by unscaled features in gradient descent?

options.text: No problem occurs, scaling is cosmetic.
The model learns the wrong target.
Features become correlated.
Slow, oscillating convergence due to poor conditioning.

questions.explanation: Unscaled features elongate the loss surface and slow convergence. They do not change the target or create correlation.

questions.topic: The ordinal imputation trap
questions.stem: Which approach best avoids the ordinal imputation trap?

options.text: Always use the mean for precision.
Use median or mode so filled values remain valid levels.
Fill with a random level.
Drop all missing ordinal rows.

questions.explanation: Median or mode keep filled values on the allowed scale. The mean risks invalid levels, and dropping is excessive for modest missingness.
